summary:
Every farmer already has a crop rotation plan for next season. Rotation-Maxxing, a free web app for US farmers, shows what that plan, and two alternatives, could really cost in dollars, soil and water before anyone plants a seed. 

You land on a spinning globe, find your farm, and watch your fields become a 3D island. Manami, our sheep guide, helps you compare your current rotation, the most profitable plan, and a plan built from your priorities, whether that's profit, soil health, water or risk. 

Your farm saves on your device with no sign-in, and an optional emailed link keeps it in an account across devices. The tool supports a farmer's judgement, not replaces it.
details:
Rotation-Maxxing shows a farmer what next season's rotation will really cost in dollars, soil and water, before anyone plants a seed.

The problem

  • Farmers are being asked to rotate crops to protect soil and water, just as the weather gets harder to predict.
  • A more diverse rotation can look expensive in the short run, and it's not obvious whether the soil, water or market will make it pay.
  • Many farms, especially smaller ones, don't have an agronomist on call to run the numbers.
  • So the same corn or soybean goes back in, even when everyone knows it's hard on the field.

Our solution

  • A free browser app with no sign-in needed: your farm saves as you go, and an optional emailed link lets you open it on any device.
    • your current rotation, continued
    • the plan that makes the most money
    • the plan that best matches your priorities (profit, soil health, water or risk)
  • The farmer still makes the call. The tool supports their judgement and doesn't replace it.

How it works

1. Find your farm

  • Land on the spinning globe and search your farm address or county, or press “Try a demo farm.”
  • Pick fields from USDA outlines, AI-detected outlines, or by drawing your own.
  • Answer three quick questions: what matters most this year, whether you irrigate, and which crops you won't or can't grow.

2. Meet your island

  • Your fields rise out of the sea as a 3D island with their real shapes.
  • It shows the real time of day, the season, and the weather happening there right now. A bell brings farm updates: frost, heavy rain, strong wind, heat and dry spells in the week's forecast at your farm, and how recent seasons' rain compares with normal.

3. Field check-up

  • Each field shows its crop history, soil, slope, rainfall and recent greenness.
  • Edit crop history: set what you really grew each year, or “Not sure.” Your years count over USDA’s in the plans, on the island, and when you ask Manami. Edits save with the farm on this device, and to your account if you are signed in.
  • Jar test: if the soil map feels off, shake soil in a jar of water, photograph the layers, and Manami reads the layers with AI (or right on your device) to work out the texture. That reading can replace the map for that field.

4. Plan your rotation

  • Build it yourself: drag crops into a three-year rotation and get instant, colour-coded warnings, like low nitrogen, the same disease family as last year, or a crop with no confirmed buyer.
  • Watch all three plans side by side and also play out on the island.
  • A sowing-and-harvest calendar uses USDA planting dates.
  • Ask Manami questions about your fields and plans in plain English. She also gives her take on which plan suits each field (always scored by the planner, never by the AI) and a short read on any field.

The engine under the hood

  • Filters out what won't work: wrong soil, no seed or equipment, or specialty crops like canola or sunflower with no confirmed buyer, each with a plain-English reason.
    • Profit: sourced USDA yields, prices and costs, adjusted for the previous crop, soil, shade from taller neighbours, and local market limits.
    • Soil health: erosion in tons per acre, ground cover from residue, and nitrogen from legumes
    • Water: how much the field actually uses
    • Risk: how badly profit drops in bad years
  • Weather-driven: replays decades of daily NASA POWER weather through a FAO-56 soil-water balance, so a dry Kansas year and a wet Iowa spring aren't treated the same.
  • Remembers soil water left over from the previous crop.
  • Found real agronomy on its own: a fallow year added about 16% to the next corn crop in dry Kansas but only about 3% in humid Iowa. We never programmed that in as a rule.

Built for trust

  • Every number is tagged as sourced data, a design choice or an assumption, with a citation.
    • Dryland Kansas sorghum tracks closely: about 0.89 correlation in Saline County and about 0.85 in held-out McPherson County.
    • Humid Iowa is much weaker, because floods, wet springs and wind aren't captured yet. Where the model struggles, we say so.
    • What we found: weather explains yield best where water is the limiting factor. In drier regions, where crop growth depends directly on rainfall, NASA weather and USDA yields line up closely. In humid regions it's more of a toss-up, because bad years there usually come from floods and storms. We combine the predicted yields with USDA prices and costs to estimate profit, and because margins are thin, those weather effects often decide which rotation pays best.

Gets better every season

  • After harvest, Manami asks how each field did: what grew, the yield, and anything that went wrong (drought, flood, hail, pests, replanting).
  • Manami compares each yield with what she expected for that season's real NASA POWER weather, and gently tunes how that field performs (hail, flood and replant years aren't learned from).
  • It re-plans the next three years while staying close to the plan already adopted.

Why it matters

  • Impact: gives any US farmer, especially those without an agronomist, an honest comparison of what they do now, what pays most, and what looks after the field - with no account required to get started.
  • Creativity: turns dense NASA and USDA data into a playful 3D island with a sheep guide and a kitchen-table jar test.
  • Validity: built on published FAO-56 and USDA methods, backtested against 24 years of real yields, and open about its limits.
  • Relevance: directly tackles Field Shift by helping farms adapt rotations to changing weather using NASA data.
